slides.narration_text: What "done" looks like this week is Lesson Blueprint v1. slides.narration_text: Let's turn to Panel 3 — Objective Alignment. The alignment chain runs left to right across each focal objective row. One: Objective. Two: Acceptable Evidence. Three: Learner Practice / Action. Four: Feedback or Use of Evidence. Five: Modality / Access Consequence. Keep that fifth link; a chain that stops at feedback is not yet an aligned plan. Guardrail: engagement, completion, confidence, and satisfaction are not automatically evidence of learning. Performance implication: learners practice the target performance before summative judgment; they do more than receive information. Scope: two focal objectives. Reuse the same objective IDs across Panels 2–5.

slides.narration_text: In this section, modality is a design tradeoff. The heading is the live Canvas title: Modality Is a Design Tradeoff. Online, live, and classroom modalities change what learners can perceive, practice, reveal, discuss, and transfer — not what tools are available. Panel 4 rule: each phase must be marked Asynchronous or Live, with an approximate duration and an instructional reason — not just tool availability. Access and cultural rule: at each consequential decision, name a likely barrier and a credible equivalent path. Point your discussion at Canvas with that exact title: Modality Is a Design Tradeoff.

slides.narration_text: Design basis — research levers. Name the research-informed practice, adult-learning principle, or course-supported design basis for consequential choices. Piskurich, chapters 10–11, pages 446–457: activity-based online learning and flipped classrooms; reserve shared time for application. Piskurich chapter 4, pages 107–128 and 173–178: compare delivery methods against learner needs, content, and constraints; sequencing and follow-up turn content into a plan. Gagné's Events of Instruction, Kurt 2021: nine events; different things are best learned by different methods; the template serves the lesson rather than forcing unnecessary steps. Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, CAST 2.2 plus Davis et al. 2022: multiple means of engagement, representation, action/expression.

slides.narration_text: We'll begin the worked example as form, not hypertension content. Maya Rivera — Strong Numbers, Trusted Conversations. Fictionality note: learner population, organization, stakeholder statements, test participants, and results are invented. Published sources are real. Follow the five-phase path: Prepare, Orient/Model, Practice 1, Feedback/Retry, Assess/Transfer. Why this works: learners practice the target conversation before assessment; every phase names its objective, evidence, feedback, and access consequence; modality carries an instructional reason, not just a tool choice; retry is short and targeted. Panel glance: Panels 02–03 held context and alignment in Week 2; Panels 04–05 are where this example lives; Panel 06 records later evidence and release in Week 4. Note: example LO-1 and LO-2 are Maya's focal objectives — not the module's four LOs. Do not conflate them.

slides.narration_text: Component register — this week equals PLANNED. Per-row fields apply to each component: objective ID; learner action; intended feedback/evidence function; planned link/location; next action; access commitment. Four rows, each PLANNED: Live Instructional Segment — Week 4 Live Instructional Segment is not a prototype. Interactive Learning Element Prototype — prototype is reserved for the Week 5 Interactive Learning Element. Assessment and Feedback Component — LO-4 touch: planned strategies may include surveys, quizzes, and performance evaluations; choose what the focal objectives require; do not build the instrument this week. Asynchronous Presentation, also PLANNED. The four components are plans at this stage and do not need to be built. Use PLANNED accurately; BUILT, REVIEWED, TESTED, REVISED, and READY are not appropriate merely because a component has been described.

selected_full_deck_preview.narration_text: Design basis — research levers. Name the research-informed practice, adult-learning principle, or course-supported design basis for consequential choices. Piskurich, chapters 10–11, pages 446–457: activity-based online learning and flipped classrooms; reserve shared time for application. Piskurich chapter 4, pages 107–128 and 173–178: compare delivery methods against learner needs, content, and constraints; sequencing and follow-up turn content into a plan. Gagné's Events of Instruction, Kurt 2021: nine events; different things are best learned by different methods; the template serves the lesson rather than forcing unnecessary steps. Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, CAST 2.2 plus Davis et al. 2022: multiple means of engagement, representation, action/expression.
